transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-12
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: 45m
Attendees: Sofia Martinez (Redwood AE), Daniel Kim (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (Hightower Head of ML), Ethan Ross (Platform Eng), Priya Nair (CFO)

Summary (auto): Quick cost/unit economics discovery covering hosted vs dedicated vs private, batching and KV/prefix caching levers, and budget constraints. Agreed next steps: pricing sheet, batching docs, run benchmarks.

[00:00] Sofia: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh this is Sofia from Redwood, with Daniel our solutions engineer. quick intro, maybe everyone on your side?
[00:12] Maya: hi i'm maya, head of ml at Hightower, we build realtime signal scoring for alt data, thanks for the invite.
[00:18] Ethan: ethan here, infra/platform, i'll be owning any benchmarking and capacity planning.
[00:22] Priya: priya, CFO, i'm mostly listening for budget and tco discussion.
[00:30] Sofia: great, main goal today is to understand your workload and constraints — latency targets, qps, expected tokens per request — and we can talk about hosted vs dedicated vs private and how that maps to per-token pricing and unit economics.
[00:45] Daniel: and i'll dig into batching, prefix/cold cache behavior, and what we recommend for cost improvements.
[00:52] Maya: sounds good. to start, our production model is a 13B transformer for signal scoring. latency target 200ms p95, avg token generation around 60 tokens, and about 250 rps peak during market open.
[01:10] Sofia: ok 250 rps with 60 tokens, got it. are these requests mostly generation or embedding/reranking?
[01:16] Maya: mostly generation + some rerank jobs batched in the afternoon.
[01:22] Ethan: our current stack is on GCP, we have a mix of a managed endpoint from a third party and some internal GPU infra. open to moving to hosted if cost-effective, or dedicated if we need predictable throughput.
[01:35] Priya: top level number for us: we have a monthly vendor budget cap of about $45k for inference, could stretch with clear ROI.
[01:44] Sofia: that's helpful — quick framing: our hosted offering has per-token pricing and we typically show customers two levers to reduce unit cost: batching (improves throughput and amortizes context overhead) and prefix/KV caching for repeated prompts which can cut token compute. Dedicated is reserved capacity with flat monthly commit but lower per-token pricing at scale; private brings VPC/HSM controls but has higher fixed costs.
[02:05] Daniel: to add, quantization options and kernel selection reduce compute cost too, but they can affect quality slightly.
[02:12] Maya: can you give example numbers? like per-token on hosted vs dedicated?
[02:16] Sofia: for a 13B-ish family model on hosted, our list per-input token might be around $0.0009 per input token and $0.0018 per output token — ballpark (depends on model). Dedicated commit often brings effective per-token down ~30-50% depending on utilization and batch sizes.
[02:33] Priya: that delta is big — but we need to model peak vs average since we have spiky usage.
[02:39] Daniel: exactly — sustained utilization is the lever. If you can sustain high GPU utilization via batching and smoothing requests (queueing short windows), dedicated looks attractive. If bursts are common and average utilization low, hosted with burst capacity can be cheaper.
[02:55] Ethan: our bursts are concentrated: 15-30min at market open and occasional end-of-day sweeps. we can share traffic histogram.
[03:02] Sofia: please do — that'll let us show a mixed strategy: hosted for bursts, dedicated for baseline. also, prefix caching: do many requests share the same prompt prefix?
[03:12] Maya: yes, scoring uses a fixed prompt template per asset with only the asset ID changing, so caching could help.
[03:18] Daniel: that pattern is ideal — with KV/prefix cache we avoid re-computing early layers and reduce consumed tokens effectively. in practice customers see 20-40% cost reduction on repeated prefixes.
[03:30] Priya: any concerns about data residency/compliance if we use hosted? we have some regulated clients.
[03:36] Sofia: hosted can meet SOC 2 and regional controls; for strict residency or on-prem requirements we'd look at private (VPC or on-prem) — that's where the higher fixed cost and setup time come in.
[03:48] Maya: ok. what about measuring true per-token cost for us — how do you model it?
[03:53] Sofia: we typically ask for a sample week of traces (tokens per request, prompt sizes, qps). we run cost-econ simulations with three scenarios: hosted only, dedicated commit with baseline util, and hybrid. outputs: projected monthly spend, latency SLO risk, and breakeven utilization for dedicated.
[04:10] Ethan: that would be great. how long does a benchmark take? and do you need our data?
[04:15] Daniel: we can run a hosted benchmark quickly with synthetic traces; for dedicated benchmarking we do a run on reserved infra — usually 1-2 days to validate batch configs and latencies. we don't need customer data — synthetic inputs that mimic token distributions are fine.
[04:27] Sofia: we'll propose a benchmark plan in the pricing doc.
[04:31] Maya: about batching — what's safe for our 200ms p95 target? we can't push latency too much.
[04:36] Daniel: short answer: micro-batching (batch windows of 5-15ms) gives good cost gains without blowing p95; continuous batching in the runtime also helps — we can tune target latency vs batch size. for a 200ms p95 we typically aim for tail latency budget of 100-150ms for compute, leaving headroom for network.
[04:53] Ethan: are there examples of config we can reuse?
[04:56] Daniel: yes, i'll share a recommended config: target batch size, max queue delay, prefetching KV cache warmup. also precompute embeddings where possible.
[05:05] Priya: CFO question — how predictable is the billing on dedicated? we need forecasting for budgets.
[05:10] Sofia: dedicated is a monthly commit (e.g., reserved GPU hours) so your invoice is predictable for commit portion; per-token for overages is at a discounted rate. we can model ramp-up discounts and commit tiers.
[05:22] Maya: what's the typical commit term? monthly, annual?
[05:25] Sofia: we do monthly and annual — annual gives better pricing. for pilots customers often start with a 3-month pilot with a smaller commit to validate.
[05:33] Ethan: any caveats on quantization and output quality? we can't degrade scoring accuracy.
[05:38] Daniel: we recommend int4 or int8 quant when quality is acceptable; we always run eval prompts against candidate quantized models. quality regressions are tracked and tied to prompt sets so you can opt to keep fp16 for critical paths.
[05:51] Maya: ok good. you're mentioning KV/prefix cache — does that require changes to our prompts or infra?
[05:56] Daniel: minimal changes: structure prompts consistently and if you can include asset context as a cached prefix that helps. infra-side, we just need request keys and TTLs; Redwood handles cache eviction and warmup policies.
[06:09] Priya: what's the expected timeline to get cost numbers after you get our traces?
[06:13] Sofia: typically 3-5 business days for a pricing TCO with scenarios; benchmark results could be sooner for hosted.
[06:20] Ethan: regarding security, we need SSO/SAML and audit logs. do you provide those on hosted?
[06:25] Sofia: yes hosted supports SAML and audit logs, plus integrations with KMS for customer-managed keys in premium plans. Private gives you full network isolation and on-prem options.
[06:36] Maya: a few quick concerns from engineering — can the runtime do continuous batching for streams and manage KV cache per-model?
[06:42] Daniel: yes, Redwood runtime supports continuous batching, per-model KV caches and configurable cache lifetimes, and automatic kernel selection based on sequence lengths.
[06:51] Maya: excellent. any gotchas for us moving from our current provider? like model compatibility or tokenization differences?
[06:57] Daniel: model variants can differ — we recommend a short model validation stage. tokenization differences only matter if you switch model families; we can map and re-eval.
[07:07] Priya: back to dollars — can you show an example with our $45k cap and expected throughput?
[07:12] Sofia: we'll run a scenario: with 250rps peak and 60 tokens, if hosted per-output token ~0.0018, monthly could exceed $45k depending on hours of peak. but with 30% reduction via caching+batching, you may hit under budget. dedicated could be cheaper if baseline utilization is high. we'll put numbers in the sheet.
[07:34] Ethan: ok. on benchmarks — we can provide a 7-day token histogram plus a sample of heavy prompts.
[07:40] Maya: yes we'll export that.
[07:42] Sofia: perfect. any competitive concerns — are you deep with any other vendors?
[07:46] Maya: we've trialed a few providers; Anthropic for some LLM tasks, and an internal infra solution. price and reliability are key.
[07:54] Daniel: noted. Redwood's angle is production economics and unified runtime across hosted/dedicated/private.
[07:59] Priya: what's the SLA on dedicated?
[08:02] Sofia: dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency targets; we'll include that in the doc for the tier we recommend.
[08:10] Maya: timeline — if we like the numbers, what's usual procurement timeline?
[08:13] Sofia: pilots can start in 2-3 weeks; enterprise procurement for dedicated/private typically 4-8 weeks depending on legal.
[08:21] Ethan: for the benchmark run, will you need us to open firewall ports or anything?
[08:25] Daniel: not for hosted benchmarks. for dedicated/private we may need VPN or peering — we will list specifics.
[08:33] Maya: ok. can you also include a sensitivity analysis: what if token size grows to 120 tokens?
[08:39] Sofia: yes we'll include sensitivity for tokens per request, QPS, and prefix cache hit rates.
[08:45] Priya: also include cost scenarios for 6 and 12 month commits.
[08:48] Sofia: will do.
[08:50] Daniel: i'll attach our batching playbook and a sample redis-ish KV cache config; it's more op notes than hard requirements.
[08:58] Maya: great. one last engineering Q — latency for cold cache on first requests?
[09:02] Daniel: cold cache is roughly the same as a full model run; but we provide warmup knobs and prefetch to mitigate. typical cold penalty is one full forward pass.
[09:12] Sophie: sorry, sofia here — small note: we'll also call out recommended quality checks when using quantization.
[09:18] Maya: got it.
[09:20] Sofia: ok sounds like agreement on next steps. recap: we'll send pricing + TCO scenarios, Daniel will send batching/caching docs, Hightower will send sample traces, and we'll schedule benchmarks week of Oct 19.
[09:33] Priya: good. thanks all.
[09:35] Sofia: thanks everyone.

End of transcript.

References shared: pricing spreadsheet (link: internal/pricing/CRM-HT-2026-104.xlsx), batching playbook (link: docs/batching-playbook.pdf), security overview (link: security/soc2-summary.pdf)
